Rodney Brooks opens his dexterity essay with Heinrich Ernst's PhD work: by 1961, he writes, Ernst had connected a computer-controlled arm and hand to MIT's TX-0 and had it picking up and stacking blocks . Hands are hard because of contact: grip force, slip and contact geometry decide success, and cameras lose most of that state once the fingers close. The five 2026 hands below rank differently by touch and by price. ## The tactile gap A review of Roland Johansson's work reports about 17,000 low-threshold mechanoreceptors in the hand's glabrous skin, roughly 1,000 of them at each fingertip . Brooks cites two videos from Johansson's lab. In his account, lighting a match took seven seconds, then four times as long once the same person's fingertips were anesthetized, with difficulty picking up and orienting the match. He says she could still sense other things in the rest of her fingers and hand and all the forces she ordinarily felt with her skeletal muscle system . In his September 8, 2025 post, Benjie Holson described limitations of the learning-from-demonstration setups he was seeing, explicitly calling them a general trend with exceptions. He pointed to the lack of good standard ways to relay wrist-force information to the human teleoperator, difficulty controlling fingers beyond open and close, and the difficulty of making human-like touch sensing available to the puppeteer. His estimate of about 1 to 3 cm of task precision was a guess from videos. He said it was likely more a teleoperation limitation than a model limitation and pointed to a video he described as showing sub-centimeter tasks . Luo and colleagues define tactile robotics as developing and integrating tactile-sensing technologies into robotic systems. Their 2025 outlook discusses challenges across sensor materials, networks, simulation, benchmarking, data interpretation, multimodal learning, and active touch . When he wrote the essay, Brooks concluded: "It looks like humanoid robots will need a sense of touch, and a level of touch sensing that no one has yet built in the lab" for tasks such as the match demonstration . ## The bet against touch Brooks frames the scaling counterargument as an imagined inner dialogue: end-to-end learning succeeded in speech-to-text, image labeling, and language models, so collecting examples of human hand use might yield dexterous control. He replies that those successes depended on engineered inputs and that dexterity learning will likely require the right sensory data and the right thing to learn . Brooks reproduces an eWeek report that describes Tesla as moving Optimus training toward a "vision-only approach" instead of motion capture suits and teleoperation. The quoted report says workers wear helmet-and-backpack rigs with five in-house cameras, record tasks such as folding a t-shirt or picking up an object, and use the videos to train Optimus to mimic those actions . Figure's September 2025 Project Go-Big announcement describes a pretraining data-collection initiative; it reports no general-dexterity result. Its initial human-video result is navigation. Helix, trained on 100% egocentric human video with no robot demonstrations for that approach, maps images and language to low-level SE(2) velocity commands, a transfer Figure calls zero-shot and, "to our knowledge", a first. Collection in Brookfield's residential environments had begun and would expand; the announcement's more than 100,000 residential units describe Brookfield's portfolio, without stating that those units were homes or trajectories collected . On three held-out episodes the mean error was 0.91 N, against 4.20 N from motor current. Their Diffusion Policy also outputs force, samples 32 actions per step and keeps the one closest to a target force from the demonstrations. On an ARX arm with no force or tactile sensor, over 15 trials per task, this raised success over a single sample from 46.7% to 86.7% for grasping an empty soda can, 0% to 73.3% for berry picking, 6.7% to 46.7% for in-hand reorientation and 26.7% to 73.3% for plug insertion . ## The bet on touch Jeremy Fishel, principal researcher at Sanctuary AI, counters that with video alone you do not know you have touched something until well after the collision has physically moved the object . Sanctuary's CEO James Wells calls touch a key enabler for creating human-level dexterity in robots . It says each fingertip sensor can detect "three grams of pressure", comparing the sensitivity to a paperclip's weight . Figure describes this as "the first time we've demonstrated neural network policies that depend on these modalities" . Touch now ships on flagship hands, Figure's included, and tactile foundation models exist, but no tactile training pipeline yet runs at vision scale. Sparsh-X pretrained on about a million contact-rich interactions from Meta's Digit 360 sensor and lifted policy success rates by 63% over an end-to-end model using tactile images . TouchWorld couples a tactile world model with a fast tactile refinement policy to reach 65% success on six long-horizon contact-rich tasks, 15.7 points over the strongest baseline . In June 2026, Dantong Niu, Yuke Zhu, Trevor Darrell and colleagues described T-Rex. It pairs a 100-hour tactile-rich dataset with a vision-language-action model that reads high-frequency touch through a variable-rate mixture-of-transformers and a temporal tactile encoder. On 12 tasks requiring delicate force control and deformable-object manipulation, its average success rate was more than 30% higher than the strongest baseline's . This world action model predicts learned tactile representations instead of reconstructing tactile images. Web-scale vision-language pretraining supplies semantic generalization, knowing what "the spatula" is in a new kitchen, as RT-2 showed for novel objects . Safety assurance is the procedure for showing that a robot system is safe enough to run. Industrial robots have a settled, numerical standards stack, but none certifies a learned policy, so what ships is a verifiable safety layer around it <Cite id="iso-iec-tr-5469-2024" />.

<span id="four-ways-to-share-a-workspace" />
## Fenceless robots use four collaborative modes, two of them quantitative

Marvel and Norcross summarise the four scenarios from ISO/TS 15066 (2016). Two are procedural: a safety-rated monitored stop permits no motion while a person is present, and hand guiding gives the operator the control channel. Two are quantitative: <Term id="speed-and-separation-monitoring">speed and separation monitoring</Term> keeps a computed distance between robot and person, while <Term id="power-and-force-limiting">power and force limiting</Term> gives up distance and bounds the contact <Cite id="marvel-norcross-2017" />.

Pick a mode under "How it keeps you safe" below, then drag "Robot speed" under "Keeps its distance". The bar under the drawing recomposes the protective separation distance from the four terms of Marvel and Norcross's NIST equation <Cite id="marvel-norcross-2017" />.

<CollaborativeOperationModes className="my-6" />

ISO/TS 15066, published in 2016, supplemented the 2011 ISO 10218 for collaborative operation and is now marked for revision <Cite id="iso-ts-15066" />. The 2025 revision of ISO 10218 integrated it normatively and introduced new classifications for collaborative applications, Hartmann and colleagues report <Cite id="hartmann-iso-10218-2026" />.

## Separation criteria assume a person approaching at 1600 to 2000 mm/s

Marvel and Norcross reproduce the ISO 13855:2010 decision criteria: an intrusion margin of at least 850 mm for a normal approach protected by multiple separate beams, against 1200 mm for a single-height beam. A two-handed control device may reduce the margin to 250 mm, but they exclude typical two-handed teach pendants from that exception and doubt that stationary-machinery criteria transfer to robots <Cite id="marvel-norcross-2017" />.

For operator approach they call 1600 mm/s a worst-case assumption and report a 2000 mm/s stationary-machinery maximum, with the 1600 mm/s option only when separation is greater than 500 mm. Approach speed may be measured directly; otherwise it is typically assumed constant and directed toward the robot. They add that 2000 mm/s may be more prudent for rapid motions and detection uncertainty, and a risk assessment may call for a faster approach <Cite id="marvel-norcross-2017" />.

The instrument is an authored teaching model whose defaults are not certified limits: C = 0.85 m, 10 m/s² deceleration, a 0.1 s reaction delay, 0.1 m position uncertainty and a 1.6 m workcell. A 100 Hz update period is 0.01 s, which says nothing about detect-to-command latency. The NIST paper calls its early-draft equation a rough approximation and requires traceable stopping-time and braking-distance measurements for a real robot <Cite id="marvel-norcross-2017" />.

## Force limits rest on measured pain thresholds by body region

Haddadin, Albu-Schäffer and Hirzinger made the force question empirical with crash-test impacts <Cite id="haddadin-2009" />. <Term id="conformal-prediction">Conformal prediction</Term> turns any model's raw output into a prediction set with a guaranteed coverage rate under exchangeability. Vovk, Gammerman and Shafer built the framework <Cite id="vovk-conformal-2022" />, and Angelopoulos and Bates's tutorial carried it into general machine-learning practice <Cite id="angelopoulos-conformal-2021" />. In KnowNo, Ren and colleagues calibrate a language-model planner conformally so that the robot asks a human for help when its prediction set is ambiguous, with a statistical guarantee on task completion <Cite id="knowno-2023" />.

The guarantee depends on what is bounded. Conformal Risk Control targets the expected value of a monotone loss <Cite id="conformal-risk-2022" />. Risk-controlling prediction sets use held-out calibration to bound expected loss at a chosen level <Cite id="risk-prediction-sets-2021" />. Adaptive conformal inference tracks coverage over long time intervals as the data distribution changes <Cite id="adaptive-conformal-2021" />. These are aggregate statistical targets; none means every individual decision is correct.

<Image id="knowno-ask-for-help-2023" />

<Term id="out-of-distribution-detection">Out-of-distribution detection</Term> asks whether the observation resembles anything the policy was trained on. Sinha and colleagues run a fast anomaly detector on the live observation stream to trigger a reactive fallback while slower reasoning catches up <Cite id="sinha-anomaly-2024" />. Runtime monitoring generalises both: Farid and colleagues detect trajectory-predictor failures by their effect on the planner, with guarantees on false-positive and false-negative rates <Cite id="farid-failure-2022" />.

Rejecting an input also requires a decision rule. SelectiveNet learns prediction and rejection jointly <Cite id="selectivenet-2019" />. Energy-based out-of-distribution detection instead scores a classifier's inputs with an energy function, addressing the overconfidence of softmax scores on unfamiliar data <Cite id="energy-ood-2020" />.

The ASIMOV benchmark tests semantic safety in robotics agents, from payload and reach limits to judging from stereo images whether a person is close enough to require a stop <Cite id="asimov-agentic-2026" />. Gemini Robotics ER 2, in public preview, reports 97.9% safety-instruction-following accuracy and 93.0% on 1 m human proximity <Cite id="gemini-robotics-er2-2026" />.

## EU rules for learned safety components apply from January 2027

From 20 January 2027, the EU Machinery Regulation lists "safety components with fully or partially self-evolving behaviour using machine learning approaches ensuring safety functions" in Annex I Part A. Its recitals call for third-party conformity assessment of such components <Cite id="eu-machinery-regulation-2023" />. The AI Act's rules for high-risk AI systems embedded in the regulated products of its Annex I apply from 2 August 2028, after the AI Omnibus extended the transition <Cite id="eu-ai-act-framework-2026" />.

## Three missing pieces block certification of learned systems

The first missing piece is a specification language in which a manipulation task's safety requirement can be written precisely enough to check <Cite id="luckcuck-formal-2019" />. The second is a humanoid standard past committee draft, giving fall risk an agreed treatment <Cite id="iso-cd-25785-1" />. The third is a published assurance case for a deployed learned system, complete enough that an outsider could dispute a specific step <Cite id="amlas-2021" />.

A position paper from October 2026, by researchers at Scuola Superiore Sant'Anna, MIT CSAIL and four other universities, asks for the same kind of evidence on the human side of the interaction. Niccolò Pagliarani, Maximilian Stölzle, Daniela Rus, Matteo Cianchetti and colleagues argue that a claim that a robot is trustworthy around people should rest on evidence for three properties in the intended setting: bounded physical risk, behavior that people can anticipate, and expectations that match what the robot has shown it can and cannot do. In their view these should guide design and evaluation from the outset, and the paper offers candidate evaluation criteria as a research agenda, with no new measurements <Cite id="trustworthy-physical-ai-2026" />.

Dexonomy starts from one human-annotated template per hand and grasp type, then refines the hand around the object in simulation <Cite id="dexonomy-2025" />. insertions.paragraph: Cloth manipulation depends on how the robot reduces the starting disorder. FlingBot learns a pick, stretch and fling primitive from visual observations <Cite id="flingbot-2021" />. SpeedFolding predicts paired gripper poses for bimanual actions, first smoothing the garment and then folding it along user-specified lines <Cite id="speedfolding-2022" />. Cloth Funnels chooses between flings and pick-and-place actions to bring garments into a canonical shape and aligned pose for later skills <Cite id="cloth-funnels-2022" />.

insertions.paragraph: Changing the tool changes the forces available. DextAIRity combines grasping and directed airflow, adjusting its blowing direction from visual feedback <Cite id="dextairity-2022" />. RoboCook models tool interactions with soft objects using graph neural networks, then combines tool classification with learned manipulation policies <Cite id="robocook-2023" />.

Separating semantic recognition from spatial control is an architectural choice. CLIPort combines CLIP's semantic features with Transporter-style spatial processing <Cite id="clipport-2021" />. RoboFlamingo uses a vision-language model for each observation and a separate policy head for temporal history <Cite id="roboflamingo-2023" />. VIMA expresses task instructions as interleaved text and images, and tests generalization in procedurally generated simulated tabletop tasks <Cite id="vima-2022" />.

The representation objective matters too. Voltron balances language-conditioned image reconstruction with image-conditioned language generation to learn both spatial detail and semantics <Cite id="voltron-2023" />. LIV learns representations and goal-conditioned rewards from captioned videos without action labels <Cite id="liv-2023" />. CortexBench found no visual representation that won every task: VC-1 led on average, while adaptation to a task or domain brought further gains <Cite id="vc1-2023" />.

insertions.paragraph: Recovery needs its own mechanism. REFLECT summarizes multisensory execution histories for a language model to explain a failure and guide a corrective plan <Cite id="reflect-robot-2023" />. Ames and colleagues combine barrier constraints with Lyapunov performance objectives in a quadratic program <Cite id="cbf-qp-2016" />.
